questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the most common actual cause of capstones failing to finish?
options: Scope failure -- being scoped for more conditions or comparisons than the available time allowed, not technical difficulty
The underlying quantum computing problem always being conceptually unsolvable
Students lacking the math skills taught earlier in the path
Hardware providers refusing all access to students
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that far more capstones fail from being scoped too large for the available time than from any single piece being conceptually beyond reach -- the fix is honest time estimation, not more skill.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say queue time should be budgeted as its own line item, separate from actual run time?
options: Running on shared cloud quantum hardware can mean minutes to hours of wait per job submission, and multiple submissions are typically needed
Because queue time is always exactly zero on quantum hardware
Because queue time only applies to classical simulators, not real hardware
Because quantum jobs never need to be resubmitted
questions.explain: The lesson explains that queue time is easy to underestimate specifically because debugging, re-runs, and additional conditions mean several job submissions, each with its own wait, not one clean submission.

questions.q: What is a 'cut list,' and when should it be written, per this lesson?
options: A pre-committed, ordered list of what to drop first if time runs short, written before building begins rather than improvised under time pressure
A list of circuits that cannot run on any available hardware
A list written only after the project has already failed
A list of co-authors to remove from the final report
questions.explain: The lesson defines the cut list as a plan decided in advance, while not under time pressure, so that a schedule slip becomes 'execute step 1 of the plan' rather than a scramble.

questions.q: In the stress-test of the Lesson 12 worked proposal, why is the 5-qubit extension placed first on the cut list rather than the 3-qubit reproduction?
options: The extension sits on top of a well-scoped core deliverable, making it the right place to absorb a schedule slip without threatening the core
Because the 5-qubit extension is less interesting scientifically
Because 5-qubit circuits are technically impossible to run
Because the proposal never mentioned a 5-qubit extension
questions.explain: The lesson explains the 3-qubit reproduction is the well-scoped, must-finish core, while the extension is additive -- exactly the kind of piece that can be dropped or scaled without threatening the core deliverable.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a scope-creep warning sign specific to quantum computing projects?
options: Adding 'just one more comparison condition' after jobs have already started running, multiplying the queue-time budget
Running the exact same circuit twice for a control and treatment group
Writing a proposal before starting to build anything
Budgeting separate time for write-up and presentation work
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists adding comparison conditions mid-project as a warning sign, since each addition multiplies the queue-time budget -- the other options describe good practices from earlier lessons, not warning signs.
